It's an intuition most developers bring from elsewhere.

shares. An Observable looks like a Promise that can emit more than once, so it's natural to assume the same model. And in the simplest case, one

The Observable is a blueprint; subscribe() runs it

. Building it does no network work at all. Angular's HTTP guide describes these Observables as blueprints for requests: the request is dispatched only when something subscribes, and each subscription is independent. The RxJS guide puts it another way: subscribing to an Observable is like calling a function. Two calls run the function twice; two subscriptions run the request twice.
Being a blueprint is also what makes the rest of RxJS useful here. You can pipe
onto the Observable before anything is sent, and they apply to every request it makes. It's why the guide's recommended service simply returns
from a method: the service describes the request, and the caller decides when, and how often, it runs.
That explains the Save button. Its handler called

and threw away the Observable it got back, so no request was ever made, and no error appeared because nothing had failed. The HTTP guide has an explicit reminder for exactly this: subscribe to mutation Observables, or they won't fire.

The blueprint model has a useful side. Unsubscribing from an
Observable while the request is in flight aborts the request, which is why an
pipe cancels a slow request when the user leaves the page, and why
drops stale searches. And once the response arrives, the Observable usually completes, so a finished request doesn't keep a subscription alive.
